guideTitle: 6 Best Magnifying Lamps for Miniatures in 2026
metaDescription: Six magnifying lamps for painting miniatures, compared by lens power, real glass clarity, light range and mounting for steady, detailed brushwork.
introParagraphs: Painting miniatures is a job of tiny, controlled movements: a highlight along the edge of a cloak, an eye the size of a pinhead, a wash that has to stop at a seam. A magnifying lamp helps because it holds the figure in sharp focus and lights it evenly, so you can see the brush tip and the paint at the same time. The wrong lamp does the reverse, with a lens so strong that the brush keeps bumping glass.

We evaluated six lamps that suit that work. The Yondlax and Drdefi are 12X real glass lamps, the Coteck and RunSenFo add a 30X inset, the Dylviw offers a gentler 5 diopter lens (about 2.25X) with 1,500 lumens, and the Coyeth is a 10X clamp lamp. The comparison looks at lens clarity, how much working distance each leaves for a brush, how well the light can be tuned for color and shadow, and how stable the mount is.

We use the usual rule that diopter divided by 4 plus 1 gives power. Prices are not quoted, and where a listing leaves out a detail such as arm length, we say so. These are comfort and convenience tools for a hobby, and they do not replace an eye examination if your vision has changed.

products.name: Yondlax 12X Magnifying Lamp, 4.3-Inch Real Glass, 84 LEDs
products.description:
The Yondlax is the best starting point for miniature painters because it balances power, clarity and light. A 4.3 inch real glass lens at 12X holds a figure in a crisp window, and glass keeps its clarity over years of use. At 12X the field is small, but a miniature is small as well, so you see the whole face or the whole shoulder at once.

Eighty-four high-output LEDs give flicker-free, even light, and five color modes with stepless dimming let you tune the tone and the intensity. Painters often prefer a neutral to cool tone for accurate color, and dim, warm light for checking shadows. The upgraded head button means you can change settings without leaning away from the figure.

The lens has no second, higher power inset, so extreme detail like pupils is harder than on the Coteck. A glass head also adds weight to the arm. Compared with the Drdefi, it has a round window and more published LED detail. Choose it as a reliable, all-purpose miniature lamp that you can leave on the bench and forget about. Set the head about a hand span above the figure, angle the light from the side opposite your painting hand, and the shadows of your brush will fall away from the work. Wipe the lens before each session, because paint mist is the usual cause of a hazy view.
products.bestFor: A general-purpose lamp for painting figures at the bench.

products.name: Drdefi 12X Square Magnifying Lamp, Real Glass
products.description:
The Drdefi is the lamp with a square window. A rectangular or square lens gives a wider view than a round one of the same height, and for painting a base, a row of rank-and-file figures or a long banner, that extra width means fewer pauses to reposition. The real glass lens at 12X stays clear and flat.

The listing stresses simplicity: a button right on the lamp does the switching, and bright, no-glare LED light is described as engineered for prolonged use. Five color modes with stepless dimming allow you to match the light to the paint and the figure.

The excerpt does not give lens dimensions, LED count or arm length, so check those on the product page. It has no inset lens for the tiniest details. Compared with the Yondlax, it offers a squarer window and fewer published figures. Choose it if you paint wide pieces or lines of figures. A square window is also kinder to batch painting, where you move along a row. Check the lens dimensions on the product page before you order, since the details we reviewed left them out.
products.bestFor: Wide pieces, bases and lines of figures.

products.name: Coteck 12X/30X Clamp Magnifying Lamp, 5-Inch
products.description:
The Coteck is the lamp for painters who chase the smallest details. A 5 inch 12X lens gives a generous window for a mid-sized figure, and the built-in 30X precision spot lens lets you check an eye, a rivet or a fine line of glaze. Having both in one head means you do not stop to change lenses.

Five color modes and ten dimming levels allow fine adjustment, and premium silicone buttons are soft and responsive. A clamp attaches the lamp to the edge of the paint desk, which leaves the surface free for palettes, brush pots and water.

The excerpt does not give an arm length, and the large head puts load on the clamp, so tighten it well. At 30X the working distance is very short, so do not paint through it. Compared with the Yondlax, it has a second lens and a clamp. Choose it for expert-level detail work. Use the 12X view for most of the figure, then swing to 30X only to check the final highlight. Remember to keep the brush well away from the glass, since the working distance at 30X is only a few centimeters.
products.bestFor: Eyes, rivets and the finest highlights.

products.name: RunSenFo 10X/30X Gooseneck Magnifying Lamp
products.description:
The RunSenFo puts a button panel on the gooseneck, close to the lens, so you can change the light without lifting your hand from the work. A 10X main lens leaves a little more working distance than 12X, and the 30X inset covers the tiniest details. For miniatures that sit on a stand, that balance is comfortable.

Stepless dimming helps tune out glare on glossy varnish, and five color modes let you pick warm or cool light. The stand holds the head on a weighted base, so the lamp sits anywhere on the bench.

At 10X the view still shows only a small area, and the arm can droop if you extend it to full reach. The lamp needs a nearby outlet. Compared with the Coteck, it has a lower main power and a stand instead of a clamp. Choose it if you adjust the light often during a session. The panel on the arm saves the small interruption of reaching for a switch with a wet brush in hand. Tighten the joint once the head is positioned so the arm does not creep.
products.bestFor: Painters who change the light often.
cons: Arm can droop at full reach

products.name: Dylviw 5-Diopter LED Magnifying Desk Lamp
products.description:
The Dylviw offers the gentlest magnification in this guide. A 5 diopter lens works out to about 2.25X, which leaves a comfortable brush distance and a wide field, ideal for basecoating, large armor panels and bigger models. The 4.3 inch real glass lens is described as distortion free.

Seventy-two LEDs deliver up to 10 watts and about 1,500 lumens, with three color modes. That is plenty of light for checking paint color and gloss. The 2-in-1 design includes a weighted base and a C-clip, so it stands on a desk or clamps to its edge.

At 2.25X it will not resolve a tiny eye or a pinhead rivet on its own, so many painters pair it with a stronger lens. The light is bright, so use dimming to avoid glare on varnish. Compared with the Coteck, it is gentler and brighter. Choose it for larger models and for long sessions. Many painters pair a gentle lamp like this with a stronger handheld loupe for the few spots that need it. The light is strong enough to check metallic paint and gloss at the same time.
products.bestFor: Larger models and long painting sessions.

products.name: Coyeth 10X Clamp Magnifying Lamp, Real Glass
products.description:
The Coyeth is the simple clamp lamp. It grips the edge of the table, leaving the surface free for paint pots, a wet palette and tools. A 4.3 inch real glass lens at 10X gives a clear, distortion-free view with a little more brush room than 12X.

Five color modes and stepless dimming handle most lighting needs, and an upgraded button on the lamp head lets you adjust light without reaching. One power, one lens and one button keep the lamp easy to live with.

The listing does not give an arm length, there is no higher-power inset, and the clamp needs a suitable table edge. Compared with the Yondlax, it clamps instead of standing. Choose it for a crowded bench or a small paint desk, especially if you already own a loupe for the finest details. Before clamping, check the table edge for a lip, a drawer or a thick apron that may block the clamp. A thin pad under the clamp pad protects a good desk.
products.bestFor: Crowded benches and small paint desks.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Painting needs room between the lens and the figure for a brush and a hand. At 12X, the Yondlax and Drdefi leave a short working distance, and 30X insets like the Coteck's and RunSenFo's leave almost none. A gentler 5 diopter lens, about 2.25X by the usual rule, leaves much more space. Choose the lowest power that shows what you need.

Brush strokes demand a flat, undistorted image. The Yondlax, Drdefi, Dylviw and Coyeth list real glass lenses, which resist scratches and stay clear. Cheaper plastic lenses can haze if wiped dry. Clean gently with a soft cloth. Avoid solvents and brush cleaner on the lens, which can cloud some coatings.

Paint color changes under different light, and a figure that looks right at the bench can look different on a shelf. A neutral to cool tone shows color more accurately, and warm light flatters but can mislead. The Yondlax and Coyeth offer five color modes, the Coteck five with ten levels, and the Dylviw three. Dimming helps you check shadows.

A paint bench is cluttered. A clamp like the Coteck's or Coyeth's frees the surface, while a base like the Yondlax's or RunSenFo's works anywhere. Think about where your palette sits. A wet palette, a water pot and a brush rack can fill a bench quickly, so a clamp lamp that leaves them undisturbed is a real benefit. Whichever you choose, keep the mount steady.
A drooping arm moves your focus. Glass heads add weight, and long arms add leverage. Keep the arm short and the clamp tight. A stable arm matters more than extra modes.

Reaching behind a base breaks your rhythm. The RunSenFo has a panel on the arm, the Yondlax and Coyeth have head buttons, and the Coteck has soft silicone buttons. Choose controls you can find without looking. With paint on your fingers, a single large button is better than a row of tiny ones. Test the buttons with a dry hand first.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power and clearance
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 5 diopter (about 2.25X), 10X, 12X and 30X lenses for brush clearance. Gentler lenses scored higher for comfort, and insets earned credit for fine detail. We also noted which lamps leave room for a brush, because a lens that forces you to paint through a few centimeters is tiring.

howWeEvaluated.title: Optics
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored real glass. The Yondlax, Drdefi, Dylviw and Coyeth list it, and the Coteck lists an optical-grade HD lens.

howWeEvaluated.title: Light
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at color modes, dimming and brightness. The Dylviw's 1,500 lumens and the Coteck's ten levels led. We also looked for flicker-free claims, since steady light matters over a long session of fine brushwork.

howWeEvaluated.title: Mount and stability
howWeEvaluated.description: We scored clamp and stand design and arm droop. Clamps freed the most space, and firm bases scored for stability. Long goosenecks were noted for droop, which spoils precision work.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The Yondlax leads on balance, the Drdefi on window, the Coteck on detail, the RunSenFo on controls, the Dylviw on gentle power and the Coyeth on simplicity. No prices are quoted.

faq.q: What magnification is best for painting miniatures?
faq.a: Most painters work between 2X and 12X. Lower power leaves brush room, and higher power shows detail. A lamp with a 30X inset helps with eyes, but is awkward for painting through. Most painters use the lower power for brushwork and the high power for checking.

A strong lens has a short working distance, so the brush tip can bump the glass. A gentler lens gives you space for your hand. Check clearance before buying. As a guide, if you can fit a loaded brush and your hand between the lens and the figure, you have enough room.

Neutral to cool light shows paint color more accurately. Warm light is gentler but can mislead. Lamps with several color modes let you check both. Painting under the same light you will display the figure in is also a good habit.

faq.q: Is glass better than acrylic for painting?
faq.a: Glass is generally sharper and resists scratches. Acrylic is lighter. All of the main lenses in this guide are described as glass.
A clamp frees bench space but needs a suitable edge. A stand works on any surface. Choose based on your desk. Many painters prefer a clamp because the bench is always crowded.

faq.q: Will a bright lamp cause glare on varnish?
faq.a: It can, especially with gloss varnish. Dim the light and angle the head. Stepless dimming makes this easy, and so does moving the lamp to the side of the figure.

faq.q: How do I keep the lens clean?
faq.a: Brush off dust first, then wipe with a microfiber cloth. Avoid solvents on the lens. Cover the lamp when idle so paint spatter and dust stay off.
